Classic invasive lobular carcinoma cells with intracytoplasmic vacuoles, harbouring a central mucoid inclusion simulating a target in the cytoplasm. (HES)

Invasive lobular carcinoma cells that lack cohesion are arranged in single-file linear cords that invade the breast parenchyma and adipocytes of the breast adipose tissue without a stromal reaction. (HES)

Classic invasive lobular carcinoma is characterized by a proliferation of cells that lack cohesion and appear individually dispersed or arranged in single- or double-file linear cords that invade the breast parenchyma. The cells have a thin rim of cytoplasm and appear rather small, albeit larger than normal breast epithelial cells. (HES)
The invasive lobular carcinoma cells are E-cadherin–negative, and the residual normal glands show a membranous expression of E-cadherin.

Pleomorphic invasive lobular carcinoma is characterized by neoplastic cells with grade 3 pleomorphic nuclei. In this example, the tumour cell density is high, and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are seen. (HES)

Invasive lobular carcinoma, alveolar pattern, with cells arranged in aggregates of ≥ 20 cells. These cells are separated by thin septa. Of note, some cells have an intracytoplasmic vacuole, some being centred by a secretion (targetoid pattern). (HES)
